Neither number is a good default, because "more agents always give better results" isn't true. Extra agents often make things worse, and they always cost more.

**A concrete case.** A student asks, "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday at 3?" One agent can do all of it:
1. Look up the student's training status.
2. Check the calendar.
3. Book the slot.

If you split that across agents, each handoff means one agent writing a summary and the next one reading it. Details get lost, and you pay for the same context to be read again each time.

**What the evidence says.** In Anthropic's write-up of their own multi-agent research system, agents used about 4× the tokens of a plain chat, and multi-agent setups about 15×. They say the multi-agent version worked mainly because it spent enough tokens on a hard problem. It won on open-ended research that splits into independent searches, and that result is from their internal evaluation, not an independent benchmark. Your assistant looks up manuals, checks a calendar and books a slot. Those steps depend on each other and don't split into independent searches. With a small sponsor budget, a 15× cost is a real problem.

**A better question than "five or ten?"** Start with one agent and a few well-described tools: manual search, calendar check, booking. Make the steps that must always happen the same way, such as checking training status before a booking, a fixed workflow. Consider a second agent only if you can name a specific job that is independent, large, or clearly hurts the main agent's context. A good test case is a huge manual search that would otherwise flood its context.

That is what you'd say at the design review: why you chose the number of agents you did, and what each extra agent would cost.

**Quick check:** name one step of the makerspace assistant that should be a fixed workflow rather than a decision the model makes. Say why.

I can also give you a lesson on workflows, agents and multi-agent systems, aimed at your budget question. Say the word and tell me how many minutes you want.

Source: [How we built our multi-agent research system, Anthropic Engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
